problem: Language-conditioned HRI and robot frameworks support only a handful of high-resource languages (English, Chinese) or rely on code-level interfaces, so most of the world's ~7,000 languages, including low-resource and vulnerable ones, cannot instruct robots.
motivation: Inclusive real-world HRI requires users to instruct robots in their native language, in speech or text, without language-specific training. Pretrained foundation models generalise across languages, but multilingual reasoning alone does not yield reliable, grounded robot actions.
key_idea: Use a frozen multilingual LLM with implicit language conditioning and a structured hierarchical action parser, combined with open-vocabulary visuo-lingual grounding and a user-confirmation gate, to map free-form instructions in any language to robot action primitives without retraining.
insight: Ablations show performance is not just the LLM's multilingual ability. Removing the hierarchical parser drops TSR from 94.32 to 69.48, removing the grounding reliability gate drops TSR to 76.31, and removing user confirmation drops TSR to 72.43 while IPA drops only to 90.22. Direct-MLLM without the structured interface gets 82.89 TSR with 32% invalid actions, and MT→EN gets 86.73 TSR, so translating first loses information.
method: Multimodal interaction interface: text or ASR speech is normalised into a language-conditioned representation (c̄_t, ξ_t), where ξ_t is an implicit exemplar of the last substantive utterance; no explicit language ID; chat GUI over ROS

Action decision and command parsing: a frozen GPT LLM infers intent, decomposes the instruction into sub-goals and produces a response in the user's language; a hierarchical semantic parser maps this to parameterised primitives (action type, object refs, spatial constraints, execution params, behavioural flags)
User-approval gate: a linear classifier over the embedding of the user's confirmation reply decides whether to execute or discard multi-step plans, and works multilingually

Open-vocabulary visuo-lingual grounding: SAM3/YOLO-World/OWLv2 masks with convex-hull quality filter, CLIP alignment with temperature softmax, energy-based rejection, degradation-aware reliability weighting, RGB-D or Depth Anything back-projection, Kalman tracking, weighted argmax target selection
Action execution mechanism: GMapping SLAM + AMCL + ROS nav for goal and object-relative navigation, twist-velocity profiles for low-level motion, and direct perception queries for query tasks
Benchmark: 140 languages (high, low, vulnerable/creole tiers), 5 task categories, 70K+ multi-turn logged interactions, GPT-based interlingual translation, 34 human raters in 13 languages

setting.backbone: GPT-4o (frozen) as instruction reasoner; SAM/SAM3, YOLO-World/OWLv2, CLIP ViT-B/32, Depth Anything as perception
setting.observation: RGB-D camera + LiDAR + odometry, plus text or speech instructions
setting.action_space: parameterised high-level primitives executed via ROS navigation goals and continuous twist velocity commands
setting.simulator: Gazebo (ROS) with an 11-room office world; also web-based simulation

numbers_note: No standard navigation benchmarks are used. The main results are per-language tables (IPA/TSR/ART) for about 140 languages; only representative rows are listed. The per-task-category and horizon results appear only in figures, and the user-study ratings appear only in a figure.
results: ReLI averages about 90% IPA/TSR across 140 languages with ART around 2.1–2.8 s. On native-speaker instructions Full ReLI reaches 94.56 IPA and 94.32 TSR, beating MT→EN (89.21/86.73), Direct-MLLM (83.46/82.89) and ReLI-Open (80.11/79.00). In the user study, over 85% of the 34 raters were satisfied with responsiveness and none perceived a language-induced gap.
limitations: Depends on cloud GPT API (latency, cost, connectivity) and inherits LLM/VLM hallucination and uneven language coverage; performance drops on scripts such as Phoenician, Cherokee, Tibetan, and Serbian

Many non-English instructions are machine-translated by GPT (a possible circularity with the GPT backbone), and IPA/TSR come from the authors' own scoring on a custom benchmark with no established baselines
Speech input is sensitive to ASR quality, noise and code-mixing; object-referenced navigation is error-prone with visually similar objects
